title: Plus-Size Men's Clothing Stores
one_liner: Specialty big-and-tall menswear stores remain relevant for fit, service and extended assortments, but 2025-2026 demand is being squeezed by e-commerce, value shopping and body-size shifts tied partly to GLP-1 use.
overview: This industry serves men who need extended waist, length, chest, footwear and fit combinations, typically including waist sizes above 40 inches, tall sizing for men above roughly 6 feet 2 inches, and apparel from XL through multi-XL ranges. The core value proposition is reliable fit, deeper size availability, larger fitting rooms, tailoring or alterations, and staff who understand fit problems that standard apparel stores underserve. The 2021 baseline framed the industry as mature and low-growth, with 2021 revenue of $848.9 million and a 2021-2026 forecast CAGR of 0.5% to $869.7 million. Current evidence points to a weaker path than that baseline: DXL, the largest specialty player, reported fiscal 2025 sales of $435.0 million, down 6.9% from fiscal 2024, and Q1 fiscal 2026 sales of $103.3 million, down 2.1% year over year. Demand support remains substantial because 2024 CDC state data show adult obesity prevalence of at least 25% in every US state and territory, but the specialty-store channel is pressured by online selection, mass retailers' extended sizes, tariff uncertainty, high occupancy costs and consumers delaying purchases while their sizes change.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimate: $800 million-$825 million in US specialty plus-size men's clothing store revenue
key_stats.growth: 2025 estimate: -4% to -6% year over year; 2026 outlook: flat to -2% if store traffic remains soft

key_stats.leader_q1_sales: DXL Q1 fiscal 2026: $103.3 million total sales, down 2.1% from Q1 fiscal 2025
key_stats.ecommerce_share: US retail e-commerce Q1 2026: 16.9% of total retail sales, up from 16.0% in Q1 2025
key_stats.apparel_retail_context: US clothing and clothing accessories store sales May 2026: $29.211 billion, not seasonally adjusted
key_stats.demand_pool: 2024 CDC BRFSS: adult obesity prevalence was at least 25% in every US state and territory; August 2021-August 2023 NHANES adult obesity prevalence was 40.3%
key_stats.price_context: BLS CPI men's apparel December 2025: +0.5% year over year; men's and boys' apparel December 2025: -0.1% year over year

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 baseline estimate: $853 million, derived from the 2021 IBIS baseline of $848.9 million and its 2021-2026 projected CAGR of 0.5%
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 baseline growth estimate: +0.5% year over year
baseline_2022.establishments: 2021 baseline: 1,211 establishments; 2026 baseline forecast implied continued contraction
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 2021 baseline: 1.0% EBIT margin; 2026 baseline forecast: 0.9% EBIT margin
baseline_2022.wages: 2021 baseline: $169 million wages; 2026 baseline forecast: $169.1 million wages

how_it_makes_money: Stores generate revenue from casualwear, workwear, denim, dress shirts, suits, outerwear, activewear, underwear, accessories and extended-size footwear, often earning higher average tickets from specialized fit, national brands and private labels. Incremental revenue comes from alterations, omnichannel fulfillment, clearance and outlet channels, loyalty programs, marketplace partnerships and seasonal wardrobe refreshes for work, weddings, travel and special events.
cost_structure: The 2025-2026 cost base is dominated by merchandise purchases, store labor, occupancy, freight, marketing and inventory markdowns. DXL's Q1 fiscal 2026 gross margin including occupancy was 44.3%, down 80 basis points from Q1 fiscal 2025, while SG&A was 45.0% of sales and marketing was 6.5% of sales. The 2021 baseline showed structurally thin specialty-store profitability, with EBIT margin at 1.0% in 2021 and a 0.9% 2026 baseline forecast, because larger stores, broad size inventories and service-intensive selling raise operating costs while price competition limits markup power.

current_dynamics: In 2025-2026, the industry is caught between a large addressable fit-driven customer base and weak specialty-store traffic. DXL's fiscal 2025 comparable sales fell 8.4%, with stores down 6.9% and direct down 11.8%, showing that even the leading specialist is not immune to discretionary softness. Q1 fiscal 2026 improved but remained negative, with comparable sales down 3.8% and stores down 4.6%. Online retail keeps gaining share, with Q1 2026 US e-commerce sales up 9.8% year over year and accounting for 16.9% of total retail sales. GLP-1 medications are creating extra size-curve volatility: Circana reported 2025 GLP-1 household usage at 23% as of September 2025, and DXL cited GLP-1 and similar weight-loss medications as contributing to structural changes in big-and-tall demand. Tariffs and sourcing volatility create another 2026 margin risk because much apparel is imported and DXL estimated enacted tariffs could reduce fiscal 2026 pre-tariff gross margin by about 100 basis points.
whats_growing: Omnichannel sales, direct-to-consumer marketing, private-label assortments, value-driven clearance, casual and performance apparel, extended-size footwear, and wardrobe refresh purchases from customers whose sizes are changing are growing. In 2026, DXL reported better conversion, higher average order value and improved direct-business performance in Q1 fiscal 2026 even as total comparable sales stayed negative. The broader online channel is still gaining share, with US e-commerce at 16.9% of retail sales in Q1 2026 and Q1 2026 e-commerce sales up 9.8% year over year.
whats_shrinking: Pure brick-and-mortar specialty traffic, small independent big-and-tall stores, slow-moving extreme-size inventory, full-price demand for discretionary apparel and legacy mall-oriented formats are shrinking. DXL's fiscal 2025 store comparable sales declined 6.9%, and Q1 fiscal 2026 store comparable sales declined 4.6%. The 2022 Economic Census showed clothing and clothing accessories retail firms fell from 56,731 in 2017 to 52,909 in 2022, illustrating the longer contraction in apparel-store operators.
recent_developments: 2025-03-20: DXL reported fiscal 2024 sales of $467.0 million and adjusted EBITDA of $19.9 million.
2025-12-11: DXL and FullBeauty announced a merger of equals targeting roughly $1.2 billion in combined annual net sales and $25 million in annual run-rate cost synergies.
2026-03-19: DXL reported fiscal 2025 sales of $435.0 million, down 6.9%, and comparable sales down 8.4%.
2026-03-23: Circana reported GLP-1 household usage reached 23% as of September 2025 and 80% of GLP-1 users expected to need new clothing due to size changes.
2026-06-03: DXL reported Q1 fiscal 2026 sales of $103.3 million, down 2.1%, and said GLP-1 medications were contributing to structural demand changes.
2026-07-20: DXL filed a preliminary proxy statement tied to the FullBeauty merger after its board reevaluated the pending transaction.
outlook: The 2026-2030 outlook is cautious. The customer base will remain large because obesity and extended sizing needs remain widespread, but the dedicated store channel is unlikely to recover the growth assumed in the 2021 baseline unless operators improve traffic, lower inventory risk and deepen omnichannel conversion. Revenue is likely to be roughly flat to modestly negative in 2026, followed by low-single-digit annual growth only if value assortments, loyalty marketing, tailoring, footwear and wardrobe-refresh demand offset online and mass-retail substitution. Profitability should remain thin in 2026 because tariffs, markdowns, occupancy deleverage and marketing spend limit margin recovery.
themes: Fit specialization versus broad retail competition
one_sentence: The US Plus-Size Men's Clothing Stores industry consists of brick-and-mortar-focused specialty retailers selling big-and-tall men's apparel and footwear, with 2025 estimated revenue near $810 million after a weaker year for category leader Destination XL and continued share leakage to online, department-store, off-price and mass retail channels.

title: Plus-Size Women's Clothing Stores
one_liner: Specialty plus-size women's apparel stores are a mature, low-margin retail niche whose demand base remains large, but whose store traffic is being squeezed by e-commerce, mass merchants and fleet rationalization.
overview: This industry consists of brick-and-mortar specialty retailers focused on plus-size women's clothing, typically sizes 14 and up, and excludes online-only retailers and plus-size sales inside department, mass-merchandise or broad apparel stores. Demand is supported by a large addressable population: CDC/NCHS data published in 2026 show 41.4% of US women age 20 and older had obesity in August 2021-August 2023, while CDC 2024 BRFSS maps show adult obesity at 25% or higher in every state. The category remains commercially important, but specialty stores face structural pressure from digital-first plus-size platforms, broader size-inclusive assortments at Target, Walmart, Amazon, Shein, Macy's and Kohl's, and specialty chains shifting customers from stores to omnichannel models. Public company data from Torrid show the current direction of travel: fiscal 2025 net sales fell 9.4% to $1.000 billion and stores declined to 483 at January 31, 2026, from 634 a year earlier, reflecting deliberate retail-store optimization rather than broad unit expansion.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: estimated US specialty-store revenue of about $6.86 billion, projected from the 2021 IBIS baseline of $6.669 billion at the 2021-2027 projected CAGR of 0.69%.
key_stats.growth: 2025: estimated about 0.7% YoY nominal/real baseline growth for the specialty-store niche, with current company data showing weaker performance among large chains because Torrid fiscal 2025 net sales declined 9.4%.
key_stats.profit_margin: 2026: baseline industry EBIT margin projected near 2.2%; Torrid fiscal 2025 operating income margin was 2.2%.
key_stats.stores: 2026: Torrid operated 483 stores at January 31, 2026, down from 634 at February 1, 2025; the older IBIS baseline projected 21,176 US industry establishments by 2026.
key_stats.demand_base: 2021-2023: 41.4% of US women age 20 and older had obesity, and 12.6% had severe obesity, according to CDC/NCHS data published in 2026.
key_stats.broader_retail_context: 2025: BLS/FRED sectoral output for US clothing and clothing accessories stores was $330.6 billion, up 5.4% from $313.6 billion in 2024.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: about $6.72 billion revenue, implied by the baseline 2021 revenue of $6.669 billion and 2021-2027 projected CAGR of 0.69%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: about 0.7% YoY projected growth after the 2021 post-pandemic rebound.
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 2022: low-single-digit EBIT margin, anchored by the baseline 2021 margin of 2.1% and 2026 forecast of 2.2%.
baseline_2022.online_pressure: 2022: percentage of business conducted online was projected to keep rising from the 2021 baseline level of 29.12%, increasing competitive leakage from physical specialty stores.

how_it_makes_money: Stores earn revenue from selling plus-size tops, blouses, bottoms, dresses, intimates, outerwear, activewear, footwear and accessories. The 2021 product mix baseline was tops and blouses at 33.7% of revenue, bottoms at 22.4%, dresses at 16.5%, other apparel at 12.0%, outerwear at 11.1% and undergarments at 4.3%. Current monetization relies on omnichannel selling, loyalty programs, private-label credit-card economics, fit expertise, replenishment basics, seasonal fashion drops and in-store fitting-room service that online-only rivals cannot fully replicate.

cost_structure.merchandise_and_freight: 2025: Torrid cost of goods sold was 65.2% of net sales, including merchandise cost, freight, shrink, merchandising payroll, distribution and store occupancy.
cost_structure.gross_margin: 2025: Torrid gross margin was 34.8%, down from 37.5% in fiscal 2024.
cost_structure.sg_and_a: 2025: Torrid SG&A was 26.9% of net sales.
cost_structure.marketing: 2025: Torrid marketing expense was 5.7% of net sales, up from 4.9% in fiscal 2024.
cost_structure.tariffs_and_sourcing: 2025: Torrid cited about $50 million of tariff-related cost impact from April 2025 tariff changes; apparel retailers remain exposed because more than 98% of clothing sold in the US is imported, according to USFIA's 2025 tariff analysis.
cost_structure.profitability: 2026: baseline specialty-store EBIT margin expectation remains near 2.2%, making rent, markdown control, freight, duties and wage leverage critical.

major_players: Lane Bryant / Cacique, owned by Sycamore Partners and overseen through KnitWell Group
Torrid Holdings Inc.
FullBeauty Brands, including Woman Within, Roaman's, Catherines, Eloquii, Avenue, Dia & Co and SwimsuitsForAll, primarily online but a major competitive force
Target, Walmart, Amazon, Shein, Macy's, Kohl's and other non-specialist competitors with plus-size assortments
Independent plus-size boutiques and regional specialty stores
current_dynamics: The core demand base is resilient, but the channel mix is unfavorable for store-only operators. Torrid's fiscal 2025 results show fewer active customers, a 7% comparable-sales decline and 151 store closures during the year, while FullBeauty's 2025 proxy materials show online direct-to-consumer channels generating about 80% of net sales, or $575.9 million. Tariffs, import compliance, freight costs and markdown pressure are limiting margin expansion, while the end of duty-free de minimis treatment for China-origin low-value shipments in 2025 raises costs for cross-border fast-fashion competitors and small importers. The specialty-store advantage is fit, bras/intimates expertise, in-person try-on and loyal repeat customers; the weakness is fixed store occupancy in a market where shoppers increasingly compare prices and size availability online.
whats_growing: Growth is concentrated in omnichannel customers, loyalty-driven retention, intimates, activewear, knit tops, dresses, denim fit solutions, extended size ranges, lower opening price points and sub-brands aimed at younger plus- and mid-size shoppers. Torrid said in its fiscal 2025 annual report that dresses grew for four consecutive quarters, while intimates, activewear and knit tops gained momentum. FullBeauty's 2025 materials point to digital marketplaces and acquired brands such as Eloquii, Avenue and Dia & Co as vehicles for reaching Millennial and younger Gen X customers.
whats_shrinking: Traditional mall-based specialty-store footprints, underproductive stores, occasion categories vulnerable to markdowns, higher-priced discretionary purchases and retailers without strong digital fit tools are shrinking. Torrid closed 151 stores in fiscal 2025 and planned up to 40 additional closures in fiscal 2026. Store-only operators are also losing share to online-only retailers, mass merchants and marketplaces with broader assortments and lower prices.
recent_developments: 2025-02-04: USFIA warned that new apparel tariffs would pressure retailers because more than 98% of clothing sold in the US is imported.
2025-05-02: CBP ended duty-free de minimis treatment for China-origin shipments under $800, raising compliance and duty costs for low-value apparel imports.
2025-07-08: Census reported clothing and clothing accessories retail firms fell from 56,731 in 2017 to 52,909 in 2022, while establishments fell from 143,534 to 121,610.

2025-12-11: FullBeauty entered a definitive merger agreement with Destination XL after expanding its plus-size portfolio through Catherines, Eloquii, CUUP, Dia & Co and Avenue acquisitions since 2020.
2026-01-31: Torrid ended fiscal 2025 with 483 stores, down from 634 a year earlier, after closing 151 locations.
2026-02: CDC/NCHS reported that 41.4% of US women age 20 and older had obesity in August 2021-August 2023.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is slow-growth and channel-shifted. Baseline revenue is still near $6.9 billion, but the strongest operators will be those that use stores as fit, service and acquisition hubs while pushing repeat buying online. Store counts among major chains are likely to keep declining through 2026 as operators close weak mall locations and redirect capital to loyalty, personalization, data-driven planning and digital assortments. Demand should remain supported by a large underserved customer base and wider cultural acceptance of size-inclusive fashion, but margins are vulnerable to tariffs, rent deleverage, markdowns and value-conscious shoppers. A practical 2026-2027 expectation is flat to low-single-digit growth for specialty stores, with share continuing to migrate toward omnichannel and online-first players.
themes: Size inclusivity becomes mainstream but also commoditized
Omnichannel replaces store expansion as the operating model
Fit expertise and intimates are defensible specialty advantages
Tariffs and import rules pressure apparel margins
Store optimization and mall exposure reshape the competitive map

one_sentence: The US Plus-Size Women's Clothing Stores industry sells women's apparel, intimates and accessories primarily in sizes 14 and above through specialty stores, with 2025 revenue estimated at about $6.9 billion and growth held near 1% as store optimization and online competition offset a large underserved customer base.

title: Podiatrists in the US
one_liner: A fragmented outpatient specialty market serving foot, ankle and lower-leg conditions, with demand tied to diabetes, aging and insurance coverage.
overview: Podiatrists diagnose and treat diseases, deformities and injuries of the foot, ankle and lower leg through independent practices, group practices, multispecialty clinics, hospitals and other medical settings. The industry is mature and highly fragmented, with demand anchored by musculoskeletal disorders, skin and ulcer care, diabetic foot care, fungal infections, circulatory issues and orthotics or related merchandise. The post-pandemic rebound has moved the industry above its 2022 baseline, but routine foot-care coverage limits and competition from primary-care physicians and orthopedists continue to cap upside.

key_stats.employment: 2025: 9,680 podiatrists in BLS OEWS national occupational data; 2024: 9,700 jobs in BLS OOH
key_stats.wages: 2025: $175,480 mean annual wage and $77.07 median hourly wage in BLS OEWS; 2024: $152,800 median annual wage in BLS OOH
key_stats.job_outlook: 2024-2034: 2% projected employment growth and about 300 annual openings
key_stats.demand_indicators: 2023: 40.1 million people, or 12.0% of the US population, had diagnosed or undiagnosed diabetes; 2024: 61.2 million people age 65+; 2025: US population estimate 341.8 million with 18.0% age 65+
key_stats.health_spending: 2025-2034: CMS projects national health expenditures to grow 5.4% annually and Medicare spending to grow 7.7% annually

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: $5.893 billion revenue in the baseline IBISWorld file
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022: musculoskeletal system and connective tissue diseases 39.9% of revenue; skin and subcutaneous tissue diseases 21.7%; other 12.6%; infectious and parasitic diseases 8.2%; endocrine, nutritional and metabolic diseases 7.6%; circulatory system diseases 5.4%; nervous system and sense organ diseases 2.8%; merchandise sales 1.8%

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes from patient visits, exams, diagnostics, non-surgical treatment, minor procedures, surgery, diabetic foot-care management, wound and ulcer care, orthotics, medications, referrals and limited merchandise sales. Payments are split across private insurance, Medicare, Medicaid where covered and out-of-pocket spending; the baseline file identified private insurers as the largest payer at 44.5% of 2022 revenue and Medicare as the second-largest payer.
cost_structure: The main 2022 cost base was clinician and support-staff compensation, with $1.917 billion of wages equal to about 32.5% of 2022 revenue, plus rent, malpractice insurance, billing and administrative overhead, marketing, medical supplies, instruments, drugs, sterilization, diagnostic equipment and IT. Profit was 14.3% of 2022 revenue. In 2025-2026, wage inflation, malpractice coverage, revenue-cycle costs and Medicare physician-fee changes are the key margin pressures; larger group practices can spread fixed overhead and negotiate payer contracts more effectively than solo practices.
major_players: Independent podiatry practices
Small podiatry group practices
Multispecialty physician groups and orthopedic groups
Hospital outpatient and health-system clinics
No national company with dominant share; concentration remains low
current_dynamics: The 2025 market is larger than the 2022 baseline, with IBISWorld reporting $7.3 billion of 2025 revenue and 2.8% 2025 growth. Demand is supported by diabetes prevalence, obesity, aging and Medicare enrollment, but many consumers still route common foot problems through primary-care doctors, urgent care, orthopedists or self-care. Medicare coverage remains important but uneven: routine foot care is generally excluded unless medically necessary or tied to qualifying systemic conditions such as diabetes, peripheral vascular disease or neuropathy. The 2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule improves the conversion factor after the 2025 cut, but CMS also finalized a 2026 efficiency adjustment for many non-time-based services, keeping reimbursement strategy central to practice economics.
whats_growing: Diabetic foot exams, ulcer prevention and wound-related care tied to 2023 diabetes prevalence of 40.1 million people
Geriatric foot and ankle care as the 65+ population reached 61.2 million in 2024 and 18.0% of the US population in 2025 Census QuickFacts
Group practices and multispecialty affiliations that share billing, marketing, equipment and payer-contracting costs
Sports medicine, orthotics and musculoskeletal treatment as patients remain active later in life
Medicare-linked demand as CMS projects Medicare spending to grow 7.7% annually over 2025-2034
whats_shrinking: Solo-practice share, as the 2022 baseline already showed consolidation away from solo practices
Low-acuity routine nail and callus care paid out of pocket when patients defer visits or use non-podiatrist caregivers
Revenue upside from routine foot care excluded from Medicare coverage unless documentation supports medical necessity
Podiatrist employment growth relative to broader healthcare practitioners, with BLS projecting only 2% growth from 2024 to 2034
Pricing power for small practices facing payer scrutiny, coding documentation demands and high local competition
recent_developments: May 2025: IBISWorld reported the US podiatry market at $7.3 billion with 2.8% 2025 growth.
Aug. 28, 2025: BLS updated its podiatrist outlook, showing 2024 employment of 9,700 jobs and 2% projected growth for 2024-2034.
Oct. 31, 2025: CMS finalized 2026 Physician Fee Schedule conversion factors of $33.57 for qualifying APM clinicians and $33.40 for nonqualifying clinicians.
Jan. 21, 2026: CDC reported 40.1 million US residents had diabetes in 2023, including diagnosed and undiagnosed cases.
Jun. 24, 2026: CMS projected 2025-2034 national health expenditure growth of 5.4% annually and Medicare spending growth of 7.7% annually.
outlook: The industry should keep expanding through 2026 as diabetes, vascular disease, arthritis, obesity and aging create steady medical need, and as broader health spending continues to rise. Growth is likely to remain moderate rather than explosive because reimbursement is regulated, routine care coverage is limited, and substitute providers handle many low-complexity foot complaints. Practices with strong diabetic-care referral networks, wound-care capabilities, surgery relationships, orthotics programs and payer contracting should outperform solo operators focused on routine visits.
one_sentence: US podiatry revenue is growing again in 2025 as chronic disease and aging lift medical foot-care demand, while Medicare reimbursement rules, primary-care substitution and wage pressure keep growth moderate.

title: Point of Sale Software Developers
one_liner: US POS software developers are shifting from register software vendors into cloud commerce platforms that bundle payments, analytics, loyalty, inventory and AI-enabled operations tools.
overview: The baseline IBIS file framed POS software developers as a growth industry with 2021 revenue of $2.779 billion and projected 2021-2027 revenue growth of about 2.24% annually; current public market estimates show faster expansion, with US POS software revenue estimated at $4.1095 billion in 2025 and $4.4999 billion in 2026. Growth is being pulled forward by cloud POS migrations, embedded payment processing, mobile wallet and contactless checkout, restaurant digitization, omnichannel retail, self-checkout and the need for real-time labor, inventory, fraud and customer analytics. Competition is fragmented at the SMB layer but increasingly platform-led, with Square, Toast, Shopify, Clover, NCR Voyix, Oracle and Lightspeed using payments, hardware, lending, loyalty and vertical software to deepen switching costs.

key_stats.growth: 9.5% forecast CAGR for US POS software from 2026 to 2033; 9.5% implied growth from 2025 to 2026 using Grand View Research estimates

key_stats.toast_scale: Toast had about 164,000 locations and $195.1 billion of GPV for 2025
key_stats.block_square_scale: Block reported Square gross profit of $3.9 billion in 2025, up 9% from 2024
key_stats.ncr_voyix_scale: NCR Voyix reported 2025 retail revenue of $1.842 billion and 2025 restaurants revenue of $818 million

baseline_2022.market_size: About $2.84 billion in 2022, derived from the baseline file's 2021 revenue of $2.779 billion and 2021-2027 projected growth of about 2.24%
baseline_2022.growth: About 2.24% projected 2022 revenue growth from the baseline file's 2021-2027 CAGR

how_it_makes_money: Operators earn revenue from SaaS subscriptions, POS software licenses, payment processing and gateway fees, hardware sales or leases, installation and professional services, support and maintenance, add-on modules for payroll, scheduling, loyalty, marketing, inventory, online ordering, delivery integrations, reporting and lending or financial services referrals. The highest-growth models in 2025 are recurring software plus transaction-linked payment revenue, because merchant sales volume raises revenue after installation.
cost_structure: Major costs include software engineering and product development wages, cloud hosting and cybersecurity, sales and marketing, payment network and processor costs for platforms that monetize transactions, customer support and implementation labor, hardware procurement for vendors that bundle terminals, and amortization of acquired technology. The baseline file estimated a 2021 profit margin near 17.5%, while current public company filings show payment-heavy platforms carrying large transaction costs and SaaS-heavy vendors prioritizing gross profit, ARR and adjusted EBITDA rather than software license margins alone.
major_players: Block / Square: Square generated $3.9 billion of gross profit in 2025, up 9% from 2024, from seller payments, software and financial services.
Toast: Toast reported about 164,000 locations, $195.1 billion of 2025 GPV and more than $2.0 billion of ARR as of 2025-12-31, making it a leading restaurant POS platform.
Fiserv / Clover: Fiserv's Merchant segment revenue grew 5% in 2025, with growth driven in part by Clover POS and value-added services.
NCR Voyix: NCR Voyix reported 2025 retail revenue of $1.842 billion and restaurants revenue of $818 million; recurring revenue represented 62% of total 2025 revenue.
Shopify POS: Shopify generated 2025 subscription revenue partly from POS Pro and merchant solutions revenue partly from POS hardware and integrated payments.
Lightspeed Commerce: Lightspeed reported $1.227 billion of LTM revenue and $98.1 billion of LTM gross transaction volume as of 2026-03-31, serving retail and hospitality merchants globally.
Oracle MICROS / Xstore: Oracle continues to sell restaurant, hotel and retail POS products including Simphony and Xstore, with 2025-era cloud, mobile ordering, payments and analytics features.
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is less about replacing cash registers and more about unifying store, online and back-office workflows. Vendors are competing on cloud reliability, payments economics, vertical depth, AI-assisted reporting, fraud controls, loyalty, handheld ordering, self-checkout, offline mode and integration breadth. Restaurants remain a high-growth vertical because POS systems increasingly manage ordering, payments, kitchen routing, delivery, payroll and guest engagement. Retailers are investing in POS systems that reduce checkout friction while improving shrink, returns and omnichannel inventory visibility.
whats_growing: Cloud-native POS, mobile POS, handheld restaurant ordering, integrated payments, digital wallets, pay-by-bank experimentation, self-checkout software, loyalty and marketing automation, AI-assisted analytics, fraud and loss-prevention integrations, vertical SaaS for restaurants and specialty retail, and subscription-plus-payments revenue models are growing in 2025-2026.
whats_shrinking: Standalone on-premise license sales, cash-only checkout workflows, paper receipt workflows, disconnected terminals, one-time installation revenue, legacy hardware-heavy rollouts and POS systems without payments, ecommerce, loyalty or inventory integrations are shrinking in strategic importance in 2025-2026.
recent_developments: 2025-05-13: The Federal Reserve's 2025 Diary reported cash at 14% of US consumer payments by number in 2024, while credit cards were 35% and debit cards were 30%.
2025-07-07: The Federal Reserve published analysis of pay-by-bank as an emerging POS merchant payment option in 2025.
2025-10-28: NRF reported retailers saw an 18% increase in average annual shoplifting incidents in 2024 versus 2023, raising demand for POS-linked fraud and loss-prevention tools.
2025-12-31: Toast ended 2025 with about 164,000 locations, $195.1 billion of GPV and more than $2.0 billion of ARR.
2025-12-31: Block reported 2025 Square gross profit of $3.9 billion, up 9% from 2024.
2026-07-01: The Federal Reserve reported 236.6 billion US noncash payments in 2024, with cards accounting for more than three quarters of noncash payments by number.
outlook: The industry outlook is positive through 2026 as merchant demand shifts toward cloud commerce platforms, embedded payments and data-rich store operations. Growth should remain faster than the baseline 2021-era projection because 2025 market estimates already exceed the baseline's 2026 revenue outlook, but pricing pressure, high customer acquisition costs, payment-margin sensitivity, cybersecurity risk and merchant churn will keep competition intense. Larger vendors are likely to keep acquiring or bundling niche software, while smaller developers can still win in vertical markets where workflow depth matters more than broad platform scale.
one_sentence: The industry develops POS software used by retailers, restaurants, hospitality operators and service businesses to accept payments, manage checkout workflows, track inventory and connect store activity with online, back-office and customer systems.

title: Polystyrene Foam Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A mature, petrochemical-linked foam converting industry is being pulled toward construction insulation while single-use foodservice foam loses ground to state bans and paper, molded fiber and reusable alternatives.
overview: The industry converts polystyrene resin and blowing agents into lightweight foam products for foodservice, institutional tableware, protective packaging, cold-chain packaging, construction insulation and transportation uses. The 2022 IBIS baseline put industry revenue at $12.381 billion, up 5.0% in 2022, with profit of $594 million and a 4.8% margin. Public 2025 market-report data indicate the broader US polystyrene foam manufacturing industry reached $13.3 billion in 2023 after a 3.0% CAGR through 2023, while EPS-only demand was valued at $1.85 billion in 2025 and is estimated at $1.89 billion in 2026. The current market is mature and cost-sensitive: construction insulation benefits from energy-code compliance and June 2026 housing starts of 1.427 million SAAR, while foodservice foam is being displaced by California, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia and other state restrictions that became effective during 2025-2026.

key_stats.market_size: 2025E US industry revenue about $13.1 billion; 2023 public IBIS/R&M figure was $13.3 billion, and 2025 EPS-only US demand was $1.85 billion.
key_stats.growth: 2026E EPS-only US demand is $1.89 billion, implying about 2.2% CAGR for 2026-2036; 2026 full-industry growth is best characterized as flat to low single digit because construction insulation offsets foodservice bans.
key_stats.employment: 2025 IBIS public snapshot: 28,953 employees, up 1.4% in 2025; 2024 employment was 28,542.
key_stats.pricing: BLS/FRED polystyrene foam product manufacturing PPI was 337.081 in June 2026, up 2.3% from 329.434 in June 2025.
key_stats.input_costs: BLS/FRED plastics material and resin manufacturing PPI was 368.751 in June 2026, up 16.2% from 317.427 in June 2025.
key_stats.construction_demand: US housing starts were 1.427 million SAAR in June 2026, up 3.5% from June 2025; building permits were 1.367 million SAAR, down 2.3% from June 2025.
key_stats.foodservice_demand: US food services and drinking places advance sales were $104.547 billion in June 2026, not seasonally adjusted.
key_stats.eps_submarket: US EPS demand was $1.85 billion in 2025 and is estimated at $1.89 billion in 2026, with building and insulation at 48.0% of 2026 demand and blocks and sheets at 63.0% of 2026 form share.

baseline_2022.growth: 2022 revenue growth was 5.0%; 2017-2022 CAGR was 2.2% in the IBIS executive summary.
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022 revenue mix: consumer and institutional products 31.7%, packaging and storing products 30.1%, building and construction products 17.3%, transportation products 6.3%, other 14.6%.

primary_revenue_streams: Selling foam cups, plates, bowls, clamshells and institutional foodservice ware to distributors, restaurants and retailers.
Selling EPS protective packaging, blocks, molded forms, cold-chain shippers and storage products to manufacturers, e-commerce, grocery and healthcare logistics customers.
Selling building and construction foam, including wall, roof, foundation and pipe insulation products, to building-material distributors, contractors and construction wholesalers.
Selling transportation and specialty foam components for automotive, appliance, electronics and industrial packaging applications.
how_it_makes_money.pricing_model: Manufacturers generally price on resin, styrene, energy, freight, labor and conversion-margin pass-throughs, with larger customers using contract pricing and smaller distributors buying catalog or negotiated SKUs.
how_it_makes_money.margin_drivers: Margins expand when plant utilization is high, resin/styrene costs are stable, energy and freight are controlled, and producers can shift mix toward engineered insulation and specialty packaging rather than commoditized single-use foodware.

cost_structure.raw_materials: Largest cost bucket; polystyrene resin, styrene-linked petrochemicals, additives and blowing agents are exposed to resin and oil volatility. Resin PPI rose 16.2% year over year in June 2026.
cost_structure.labor: 2022 baseline wages were $1.736 billion, equal to about 14.0% of 2022 revenue.
cost_structure.profit: 2022 baseline profit was $594 million, or 4.8% of revenue; 2025-2026 margins are pressured by resin inflation and compliance costs but supported by price pass-throughs.
cost_structure.energy_and_utilities: Material because foam expansion, molding, extrusion, drying and plant climate systems require heat, electricity and compressed air.
cost_structure.freight_and_logistics: High relative to product value because foam is bulky and low-density, making shipping distance, densification and regional plant footprint critical.
cost_structure.compliance_and_recycling: Rising cost item in 2025-2026 as state EPS restrictions, EPR laws, customer sustainability requirements and take-back/recycling programs require monitoring, reporting and alternative-material development.

current_dynamics: 2025-2026 demand is bifurcating: building insulation and engineered packaging are more defensible, while single-use EPS foodservice ware is losing addressable volume in regulated states.

Input costs have turned adverse again: plastics material and resin PPI was up 16.2% year over year in June 2026, while polystyrene foam output prices were up only 2.3%, implying margin pressure where contracts lag costs.
Construction is mixed but supportive for insulation: June 2026 housing starts rose 3.5% year over year, but permits fell 2.3%, suggesting near-term insulation demand with a softer forward pipeline.

Foodservice sales remain large, with June 2026 food services and drinking places sales at $104.547 billion, but more of that packaging demand is shifting to paper, molded fiber, polypropylene, PET and reusable formats.

State regulation is now the largest structural headwind for foodservice EPS, with California and Oregon restrictions effective January 1, 2025, Rhode Island effective January 1, 2025, Virginia broadening to all food vendors on July 1, 2026, and New York adding a cold-storage EPS container ban on January 1, 2026.
whats_growing: EPS and XPS-style insulation boards for walls, roofs, foundations and below-grade applications tied to energy-code compliance and retrofit demand.
Blocks and sheets: 63.0% of US EPS form share in 2026, supported by construction and flat-board insulation uses.
Building and insulation demand: 48.0% of US EPS application share in 2026.
Geofoam, cold-chain protective packaging, reusable transport packaging and engineered molded foam where performance, insulation and damage reduction matter more than single-use optics.
Recycling, densification and take-back services as producers try to defend foam’s environmental position and satisfy EPR/customer requirements.
whats_shrinking: Single-use EPS cups, plates, clamshells and takeout containers in California, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, New York, New Jersey, Colorado, Washington and other restricted jurisdictions.
Loose-fill EPS packaging peanuts where state bans and parcel reuse alternatives reduce demand.
Commodity foodservice foam sold through restaurants and distributors that can switch to paper, molded fiber, coated board, PET, PP or reusable systems.
Long-haul shipment of low-density foam products, because freight economics favor regional production, densification or substitution.
recent_developments: 2025-01-01: California EPS foodservice ware sales and distribution restrictions took effect unless producers could demonstrate a 25% EPS recycling rate; CalRecycle says the threshold has not been met.
2025-01-01: Oregon prohibited food vendors from using polystyrene foam prepared-food containers and prohibited sales of polystyrene foam containers and packaging peanuts.
2025-01-01: Rhode Island prohibited covered establishments from providing food or beverages in disposable food service containers made wholly or partly of polystyrene foam.
2025-07-01: Virginia’s EPS food container ban began applying to chain food vendors with 20 or more locations, ahead of the broader July 1, 2026 phase-in for all food vendors.
2026-01-01: New York’s expanded polystyrene ban added cold-storage containers such as certain foam coolers and ice chests.
2026-06-01: BLS/FRED polystyrene foam product manufacturing PPI reached 337.081, up 2.3% from June 2025, while resin input PPI was up 16.2% year over year.
outlook: The 2026-2030 outlook is slow growth to flat for the broader industry and modest growth for construction EPS. EPS-only US demand is forecast at a 2.2% CAGR from 2026 to 2036, reaching $2.35 billion by 2036, but the foodservice foam category faces a structurally smaller addressable market as state bans, EPR rules and retailer sustainability policies expand. Producers with regional plant networks, insulation-grade products, engineered packaging, resin pass-through contracts and credible recycling/take-back systems should outperform commodity foodware converters. Key risks are resin/styrene inflation, freight costs, construction-cycle weakness, and further state or federal restrictions on single-use polystyrene.
themes: Regulatory substitution away from single-use EPS foodware
Construction insulation as the defensive growth engine
Petrochemical and resin price pass-through risk
Regional manufacturing footprint and freight economics
Packaging mix shift toward paper, molded fiber, PP, PET and reusable systems
